title: Yoga Calorie Burn Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Calories Burned in Yoga by Style
description: Calculate calories burned during yoga. Free calculator for hatha, vinyasa, ashtanga, bikram & yin styles based on weight & duration.
intro: How many calories does a yoga class actually burn? Less than most people think — and that's fine, because torching calories isn't the point of yoga. This calculator uses MET values (Metabolic Equivalent of Task) from the Ainsworth Compendium of Physical Activities (2011), the gold-standard reference used by ACSM and the CDC. Each yoga style has a published MET value: gentle Hatha sits at 2.5 MET, Vinyasa flow at 3.3 MET, Power Yoga at 4.0 MET, Bikram and hot yoga around 4.0 MET, Ashtanga 4.0+ MET, and Yin or Restorative at 2.0 MET. The formula is straightforward: kcal/min = MET × 3.5 × kg / 200. For a 150-lb (68 kg) practitioner, a 60-minute Vinyasa class burns about 235 kcal — roughly half what the same hour of moderate running would burn. The 'yoga is low intensity' label is misleading though: yoga's primary benefits aren't caloric — they're strength, balance, flexibility, joint mobility, breath control, and stress regulation. Use this calculator to estimate yoga's contribution to your daily energy expenditure, then layer strength training and cardio for body composition goals.
keyTakeaway: Formula: **kcal/min = MET × 3.5 × kg / 200**. Hatha 2.5 MET, Vinyasa 3.3 MET, Power 4.0 MET, Bikram 4.0 MET, Ashtanga 4.0+ MET, Yin 2.0 MET (Ainsworth Compendium 2011).

explanation:
## The MET formula behind yoga calorie burn

The calculation is the same one ACSM, CDC, and exercise physiology textbooks use for every activity:

**kcal/min = MET × 3.5 × body weight (kg) / 200**

Where MET (Metabolic Equivalent of Task) is the ratio of working metabolic rate to resting metabolic rate. 1 MET ≈ 3.5 ml O₂/kg/min, the oxygen consumption of quiet sitting. A 3 MET activity uses three times the energy of sitting still. The Ainsworth Compendium of Physical Activities (2011, *Med Sci Sports Exerc*) is the reference database that assigns MET values to every codified activity, including the major yoga styles.

## Calories burned by style — worked examples for a 150-lb (68 kg) practitioner

| Style | MET | Typical duration | Kcal burned |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hatha (gentle) | 2.5 | 60 min | (2.5 × 3.5 × 68 / 200) × 60 = **178 kcal** |
| Vinyasa flow | 3.3 | 60 min | (3.3 × 3.5 × 68 / 200) × 60 = **235 kcal** |
| Power Yoga / CorePower C2 | 4.0 | 60 min | (4.0 × 3.5 × 68 / 200) × 60 = **285 kcal** |
| Bikram (90-105°F) | 4.0 | 90 min | (4.0 × 3.5 × 68 / 200) × 90 = **428 kcal** |
| Ashtanga (Primary Series) | 4.0+ | 90 min | ~**428 kcal** |
| Yin / Restorative | 2.0 | 75 min | (2.0 × 3.5 × 68 / 200) × 75 = **178 kcal** |

Heavier practitioners burn proportionally more: a 180-lb (82 kg) person burns ~20% more kcal at every MET.

## The hot yoga myth: sweat ≠ extra calories

This comes up in every Bikram studio. The reasoning sounds plausible — 'I'm sweating through three towels, I must be incinerating calories.' The evidence says no. Tracy and colleagues (*J Strength Cond Res*, 2014) measured energy expenditure during a standard 90-minute Bikram class and found values consistent with normothermic Vinyasa at room temperature. Most of the sweat is passive — your body cooling itself in a 105°F room, not metabolic work. The scale drops 2-4 lb post-class because of fluid loss, not fat loss. Rehydrate and it comes right back. Hot yoga still has real benefits (heat-induced vasodilation, improved flexibility from warmer connective tissue, mental discipline of working in heat), but extra caloric burn isn't one of them.

## The US yoga landscape (2026)

Yoga Alliance is the dominant US certification body — look for RYT-200 (200-hour minimum) or RYT-500 credentials on your teacher's bio. CorePower Yoga has nationwide studios (C1 = Hatha foundation, C2 = Vinyasa power flow, Sculpt = power yoga + weights, Hot Power Fusion = heated). YogaWorks closed its corporate studios in 2020 post-bankruptcy but some independent locations continue. Drop-in classes run $20-30 in most US cities, $25-40 in NYC, SF, and LA. Class packages bring it to $15-22 per class. Apps like Glo, AloMoves, and Down Dog are $13-20/month and have replaced studio attendance for many practitioners since 2020.

## Style breakdown — what you're actually doing

- **Hatha** — slow, alignment-focused, longer holds. The on-ramp for beginners. Sanskrit: hatha just means 'physical practice.'
- **Vinyasa** — flow style, breath-paced movement, every inhale and exhale linked to a transition. Variable intensity by teacher.
- **Ashtanga** — Pattabhi Jois lineage, set Primary Series practiced in sequence, traditionally taught Mysore-style (self-paced with teacher adjustments).
- **Iyengar** — B.K.S. Iyengar lineage, prop-heavy (blocks, straps, bolsters, walls), precision-driven alignment, long holds.
- **Bikram / Hot 26** — Bikram Choudhury's set sequence of 26 postures + 2 breathing exercises, 90 minutes, 105°F room. (Bikram-branded studios shrank after the founder's misconduct lawsuits; many rebranded 'Hot 26' or 'Original Hot Yoga.')
- **Yin** — passive floor poses held 3-5 minutes, targets connective tissue and fascia rather than muscle.
- **Restorative** — fully prop-supported, near-zero muscular effort, parasympathetic nervous system reset.

## Benefits beyond calories — what actually matters

The peer-reviewed evidence base for yoga's non-caloric benefits is genuinely strong:

- **Low back pain**: Sherman et al. (*Arch Intern Med*, 2011) RCT of 228 adults with chronic low back pain — yoga was as effective as stretching classes and better than self-care book, with improvements lasting through 26-week follow-up.
- **Depression and anxiety**: Cramer et al. meta-analysis (*Depress Anxiety*, 2013) found yoga significantly reduced depression severity compared to usual care.
- **Fall prevention in older adults**: Tiedemann et al. (*J Am Geriatr Soc*, 2013) — 12-week yoga program improved balance and reduced fall risk in adults 60+.

## Props worth buying

For a home practice (or to bring to studios that don't supply props):
- **Mat**: Manduka PRO ($120, lifetime), Lululemon The Mat 5mm ($88), Gaiam basic ($20-30). For sweaty hot yoga, add a Yogitoes towel ($60).
- **Blocks**: $10-20 cork or foam, buy a pair.
- **Strap**: $10-15 cotton with D-ring buckle.
- **Bolster**: $40-60 for Restorative and Yin.

## Bottom line

Yoga's MET values are honest — gentle styles burn ~150-180 kcal/hour for a 150-lb practitioner, vigorous styles 280-430 kcal. That's modest compared to running (10-min mile ≈ 700+ kcal/hour) or strength training with short rest periods. For body composition, treat yoga as supplementary cardio and an active recovery tool, not your primary fat-loss driver. For everything else yoga is good for — and that list is long — the kcal number is beside the point.

faq.q: Do you really burn more calories in hot yoga?
faq.a: No, not meaningfully. Tracy et al. (*J Strength Cond Res*, 2014) measured Bikram class energy expenditure and found it similar to room-temperature Vinyasa. The heat (90-105°F) makes you sweat heavily, but sweat is passive cooling, not metabolic work. The 2-4 lb you lose during a hot class is water, not fat — it returns with one bottle of Gatorade.

faq.q: Is yoga enough exercise on its own?
faq.a: It depends on your goals. For cardiovascular health, the CDC recommends 150 min/week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 min/week of vigorous activity. Vinyasa, Power, Bikram, and Ashtanga count toward moderate-intensity. For body composition (fat loss + muscle gain), most exercise physiologists recommend adding 2-3 sessions/week of resistance training. For flexibility, balance, mobility, and stress regulation, yoga alone is sufficient.

faq.q: What's the difference between Vinyasa and Power Yoga?
faq.a: Vinyasa is the broader category — any flow-style class linking breath to movement. Power Yoga is Vinyasa's more intense cousin, popularized in the US by Beryl Bender Birch and Bryan Kest in the 1990s and now the signature format at CorePower (their C2 and Sculpt classes). Power Yoga uses Ashtanga's vigorous pace without the strict set sequence. MET-wise, Vinyasa averages 3.3 and Power 4.0+.

faq.q: Which yoga style should a complete beginner start with?
faq.a: Hatha or beginner-level Vinyasa. Hatha moves slowly enough to learn alignment (mountain pose, downward dog, warrior I/II, child's pose) without rushing. Avoid Ashtanga, Bikram, and Power Yoga for the first month — they assume you already know the basic postures. CorePower's C1 class or any studio's 'Yoga Foundations' series is a solid on-ramp. Apps like Glo and AloMoves have explicit beginner tracks.

faq.q: Is it safe to do yoga every day?
faq.a: Yes, for most styles. Daily Hatha, Yin, or Restorative is fine and arguably ideal — these aren't muscle-damaging activities, so recovery isn't a constraint. Daily vigorous practice (Power, Ashtanga, Bikram) is fine for experienced practitioners but rotate styles to avoid overuse injuries to wrists and shoulders (both take repeated load in chaturanga, the yoga push-up). One vigorous + six gentle is a sustainable weekly pattern.

faq.q: Does yoga help with weight loss?
faq.a: Indirectly, yes. Yoga alone burns modest kcal (Vinyasa ~235 kcal/hour for a 150-lb person), so it's not a primary fat-loss driver. But yoga's documented effects on stress, sleep, and mindful eating (Lauche et al., *Prev Med*, 2016) help with the behavioral side of weight management. The reliable path: caloric deficit through diet + resistance training to preserve muscle + yoga 2-3x/week for stress and recovery.

faq.q: Is yoga different for men vs women?
faq.a: Same physiology, same MET values, same kcal burn at the same body weight. The cultural perception that yoga is 'for women' is American-specific — globally and historically yoga was practiced predominantly by men. Yoga's strength benefits (especially Ashtanga and Power) translate well for any athlete. The US is gradually catching up; CorePower and Y7 both report rising male attendance.

faq.q: Why does my Apple Watch say I burned way more calories than this calculator?
faq.a: Apple Watch, Fitbit, and Garmin overestimate yoga calorie burn — by 30-50% in most cases. Their algorithms use heart rate and motion to estimate effort, but yoga's static holds keep heart rate moderate while engaging muscles in ways the wearable can't see. The MET-based calculation here is closer to lab-measured indirect calorimetry values. Trust the MET formula over the watch for yoga; trust the watch for running and cycling.
